39-033.r: Sea cow and sea lion → mammals; seahorse → a small marine bony fish.
39-033.t: Don't let the 'sea' names mislead: seahorse is a fish, sea cow and sea lion are mammals.

39-034.r: Dolphins → aquatic mammals (toothed whale family), carnivores eating fish and squid; Ganga Dolphin is India's national aquatic animal.

39-035.r: Seal → semi-aquatic carnivorous mammal; group pinnipeds (= fin-footed); eats fish, crustaceans, shellfish.

39-036.r: Gavialis (Gharial), family Gavialidae → mostly found in the Ganga river; breeding populations in Bangladesh, Nepal and India.

39-037.r: Otter (subfamily Lutrinae, family Mustelidae) → the 'atrocious' animal among penguin, whale, otter and tortoise.

39-038.r: Hedgehog and pangolin roll up into a ball to protect vulnerable parts from predators; marmot does not.
39-038.h: Hedgehog's spines point outwards when rolled; pangolin's scales do the same job.

39-039.r: Indian squirrels: build nests (dreys) in trees, not ground burrows (statement 1 wrong); store nuts and seeds in the ground; omnivorous → only two correct.

39-040.r: Dingo (Canis lupus dingo, Australia) → cannot bark; it howls like a wolf.

39-041.r: Bear seen performing on streets → Sloth bear.

39-042.r: Chimpanzee, parrot and dolphin have been taught to use language with some success; dog has not.

39-043.r: Desire to learn (and ability to express) separates humans from apes.

39-044.r: Langur → long-tailed Asian monkey (subfamily Colobinae), not an ape; apes (Hominoidea: gibbon, gorilla, orangutan, chimpanzee, humans) have no tail.

39-045.r: Smallest man-like ape → Gibbon ('lesser ape'); gorilla, chimpanzee and orangutan are the 'great apes'.

39-046.r: Orangutan → uses a stick as a tool to scrape insects from tree holes and poke logs for honey.

39-048.r: Amphibians → live both in water and on land (Greek 'amphibios' = both kinds of life); cold-blooded ectotherms.

39-049.r: Frog → breathes through its thin, permeable skin rich in blood vessels (skin respiration); it is an amphibian.

39-050.r: Frogs are cold-blooded (True); so are snakes, lizards, fish and crocodiles.

39-051.r: Frog metamorphosis → intestine shortens; thyroid hormone controls remodelling of the tadpole intestine.

39-052.r: Three-chambered heart (2 atria + 1 ventricle) → frog/amphibians and most reptiles; fish 2 chambers; monkey and crocodile 4.
39-052.t: Crocodile is the reptile with a four-chambered heart.

39-054.r: A true: amphibians tolerate mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in their single ventricle. R false: two-chambered heart belongs to fishes; amphibians have three.

39-055.r: No gallbladder in camel, giraffe, rat and some fish (also equines, elephants, rhinos, whales, doves, most deer) → book gives no single answer (*).

39-056.r: Jackal (Canis aureus, family Canidae) → padded feet with nails, no hooves; deer, zebra and horse are hoofed.

39-057.r: Nilgai → largest Asian antelope, of family Bovidae (cow family), not a true deer (Cervidae). Book's answer: deer family.
39-057.c: Nilgai is an antelope of the family Bovidae, the cow family (same subfamily as cattle); deer are Cervidae. So (a) Cow is scientifically correct; the book keys (d) Deer.

39-058.r: Asiatic wild ass → Equus hemionus; Barasingha → Cervus duvaucelii; Chinkara → Gazella bennettii; Nilgai → Boselaphus tragocamelus.

39-059.r: Leopard → Panthera pardus; lion P. leo, tiger P. tigris, snow leopard P. uncia, jaguar P. onca.

39-060.r: Correct: lions have no particular breeding season; cheetahs, unlike most big cats, do not roar (they growl). Wrong: statement that male leopards don't scent-mark territory.

39-061.r: Marsupials (pouched mammals: kangaroo, koala, opossum, wombat) are not naturally found in India (I correct); 'thrive only in predator-free montane grasslands' is wrong (II).

39-062.r: Wingless insect → Silverfish; flightless bird → Kiwi; limbless reptile → Snake; lungless creature → Fish.

39-063.r: Kiwi → flightless bird found only in New Zealand (genus Apteryx).

39-064.r: Coral → organic origin: marine Cnidaria polyps that secrete a calcium carbonate skeleton; emerald, ruby, topaz are not organic.

39-065.r: Octopus → cephalopod mollusc (order Octopoda), also called devilfish; two eyes, four pairs of arms.

39-066.r: Largest invertebrate → colossal squid (maximum size 12-14 metres).

39-067.r: Crab → class Malacostraca; mite, scorpion and spider → class Arachnida. So crab is the odd one.

39-068.r: White Leghorn → a variety of fowl (chicken).

39-069.r: Ticks and mites → Arachnids (4 pairs of legs; abdomen not externally segmented).

39-070.r: Termites (eusocial insects, infraorder Isoptera) → also called 'white ants'.

39-071.r: Glow-worm → a luminous insect (not a worm); its larva gives off light.

39-072.r: Female Anopheles rests at an angle to the surface (abdomen up); female Culex rests parallel to it.

39-073.r: Peacock (Gooty) tarantula, Poecilotheria metallica → insectivorous, arboreal spider, not a crustacean; in India found only in some forest areas; Critically Endangered.

39-074.r: Spider → arachnid (8 legs, 2 body segments, no wings or antennae), not an insect; bed bug, housefly, mosquito are insects with 6 legs.

39-077.r: Spider silk (a protein fibre, both strong and elastic) → 'Gossamer silk'.
39-077.t: Tussar, Munga and Ahimsa silk are not spider silk.

39-078.r: Silkworm yields silk of commerce at the pupa stage, when it spins a cocoon of one continuous strand about 1.5 km long.

39-079.r: Silkworm (larva of silkmoth Bombyx mori) → grows on mulberry leaves.

39-080.r: Lac → resinous secretion of lac insects (Kerria lacca); used to make varnishes. Pearl, coral and gum are not insect secretions.

39-081.r: Pearl → made inside molluscs (pearl oysters Pinctada, freshwater mussels), not insects; silk, honey and lac come from insects.

39-082.r: Helicoverpa armigera (cotton bollworm) → harmful pest of 100+ crops; beneficial: Bombyx mori (silk), Laccifer lacca (lac), Apis mellifera.

39-083.r: Cockroach → white/colourless blood (no haemoglobin); oxygen reaches tissues through tubes called tracheae.

39-084.r: Earthworm → no red blood cells; blood is red due to haemoglobin (erythrocruorin) dissolved in plasma.

39-085.r: Earthworms → farmers' friends, improve soil fertility (1 correct); they have about five pairs of heart-like aortic arches in segments 7-11, not two (2 wrong).

39-086.r: Dolphins and whales breathe air through a blowhole; earthworms breathe through their skin → both correct.

39-087.r: Most insects respire through a tracheal system (a network of tubes), not lungs, gills or skin.

39-088.r: Cicada, froghopper and pond skater → insects; cicadas (order Hemiptera, true bugs) are 3,000+ species of sound-producing insects.

39-089.r: Tapeworm → hermaphrodite; roundworm → separate sexes; filaria → caused by a nematode; guinea worm (Dracunculus medinensis) → a nematode, not an annelid.

39-090.r: Detritivores (eat dead or decaying matter) → earthworms, millipedes, woodlice; not jellyfish or seahorses.

39-091.r: Oyster → filter feeder (strains food particles from water); filter feeders clarify water and are called ecosystem engineers.

39-092.r: Parasitoid → lays eggs on or inside a host; larvae feed on it and finally kill it (endo- and ectoparasitoids); found in only three of the five groups.

39-093.r: Nocturnal (active at night) → mosquito, bat, owl, kiwi.

39-094.r: Lion-tailed macaque (Macaca silenus, endemic to Western Ghats) → diurnal, sleeps at night in trees; book counts only one of the three as nocturnal.
39-094.c: UPSC's official key is (a) Only one, as printed: the sambar is treated as crepuscular (dawn and dusk) rather than mainly nocturnal, leaving only the Malabar civet.

39-095.r: Largest brain in proportion to body size → ant. Largest brain overall → sperm whale (about 7 kg); human brain about 1.2 kg.

39-096.r: Ant bite → injects formic acid (a simple carboxylic acid).

39-097.r: Ants (e.g. leafcutter ants, tribe Attini) → cultivate fungi as food, like humans farm crops (ant-fungus mutualism).

39-098.r: Only female mosquitoes suck blood (males feed on flower and fruit juices); females are larger, with bigger wings → statements 2 and 5.

39-099.r: Camel ('Ship of the Desert') → stores water in its intestine; can drink more than 100 litres at once.

39-100.r: Kangaroo rat (North American desert rodent) → lives longest without drinking water; most concentrated, almost solid urine of all mammals.

39-102.r: Spider → female often kills and eats the male before, during or after copulation (spider cannibalism).

39-103.r: King Cobra → only snake that builds a nest; oviparous female lays 20-40 eggs in a leaf mound and guards it until hatching.

39-105.r: Cobra venom → mainly neurotoxic (affects nervous tissue); also has cardiotoxic compounds; toxins are proteins and polypeptides.

39-106.r: King Cobra → diet mainly other snakes (rat snakes, small pythons, cobras, kraits).

39-107.r: Python (family Pythonidae) → non-venomous snake; cobra, viper and coral snake are venomous.

39-108.r: Snake venom glands → homologous to the salivary glands of vertebrates; venom is refined saliva.

39-109.r: Snake's poison fangs → modified maxillary teeth of the upper jaw, attached to poison glands.

39-110.r: Poisonous species exist among butterflies (e.g. Monarch, toxins from caterpillar food plants), fish and frogs → all three.

39-111.r: All true: green sea turtle (herbivore), parrot fish (eats algae), dugong (herbivorous marine mammal), green anaconda (viviparous snake).

39-112.r: Dogs are not herbivores (False); evidence shows they are natural carnivores.

39-113.r: Largest flower → Rafflesia (Rafflesia arnoldii; no leaves, roots or stem), described by Sir Stamford Raffles in 1818.

39-114.r: Insectivorous plants grow in nitrogen-deficient soil; they trap insects to meet their nitrogen need.

39-115.r: Pitcher plant → insectivorous (carnivorous) plant; gets nitrogen from the insects it traps.

39-116.r: Pitcher plant → its leaf is modified into the pitcher, a pitfall trap for prey.

39-117.r: Wrong pair: Nepenthes – parasitic angiosperm; pitcher plant photosynthesises (autotroph) and digests insects for nitrogen. Correct: yeast–fermentation, casein–milk protein, Aloe vera–angiosperm.

39-118.r: Nepenthes → insectivorous pitcher plant, often in acidic soil; not Nyctanthes, Nelumbo or Nicotiana.

39-119.r: Nepenthes khasiana (India's only pitcher plant) → Meghalaya: Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills; named after the Khasi Hills.

39-120.r: Turmeric (Curcuma longa, ginger family Zingiberaceae) → obtained from a modified underground stem, the rhizome.

39-124.r: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas, family Convolvulaceae) → a modified root, grown by vegetative propagation.

39-125.r: Sweet potato stores food in a root (developed from the radicle); sugarcane, potato and ginger store food in modified stems.

39-126.r: Ginger → modified stem; turnip, carrot and sweet potato → modified roots.

39-127.r: Ginger is a stem, not root, because it has nodes and internodes (with scaly leaves); potato (tuber), garlic (bulb), yam (corm) are also stems.

39-128.r: Rhizome → ginger; tuber → potato; bulb → garlic; corm → Jimikand (suran).
39-128.t: Don't confuse corm (Jimikand, colocasia, crocus) with bulb (onion, garlic) or rhizome (ginger, turmeric, sugarcane).

39-129.r: Potato (Solanum tuberosum, nightshade family Solanaceae) → modified stem called a tuber, storing starch.

39-131.r: Pea plant → dicot herbaceous annual (a herb), family Fabaceae (Leguminosae); prefers cool damp weather, 60-75 °F.

39-132.r: Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea), horse-gram (kulthi) and soybean → all three in the pea family, Fabaceae (Leguminosae, legumes).

39-133.r: Clove → aromatic closed, dried flower bud of Syzygium aromaticum (family Myrtaceae), native to Indonesia.

39-139.r: Wrong pair: Saffron – Seed; saffron comes from styles and stigmas of the Crocus sativus flower. Correct: ginger–rhizome, opium–capsule, jute–stem.

39-140.r: Saffron → dried stigmas and styles (gynoecium, the seed-forming parts) of the Crocus sativus flower.

39-141.r: Wrong pair: Potato – Roots; potato's edible part is a tuber (modified stem). Correct: ginger–rhizome, onion–fleshy leaves, coconut–endosperm.

39-143.r: Ladies finger (okra, Abelmoschus esculentus, mallow family) → a fruit (capsule up to 18 cm); potato is a tuber, radish and sweet potato are roots.

39-144.r: Apple → false fruit (from ovary plus other flower parts), like cashew and pear; true fruits (from ovary only): grape, date, plum, mango.

39-145.r: Lychee (soapberry family) → a drupe, like plum, cherry and mango.

39-146.r: Mango (a drupe) → edible part is the fleshy mesocarp; epicarp is the peel, endocarp the hard stone.

39-147.r: Garlic's smell → sulphur compounds (allyl methyl sulphide).

39-148.r: Onion makes you cry → it releases sulfenic acid, which irritates the lachrymal (tear) glands.

39-149.r: Pungency of chillies → capsaicin, an alkaloid extracted from chillies and also used in medicine.

39-150.r: Red chillies are hot → capsaicin; not ricin, arecoline or caffeol.

39-151.r: Sweet taste of fruits → fructose ('fruit sugar'), a monosaccharide.

39-152.r: Diatoms (photosynthetic algae of almost all waters) → used in forensics to diagnose death by drowning.

39-153.r: Mulberry fruit → sorosis: a multiple fleshy fruit formed from ovaries of many flowers; pineapple is also a sorosis.
39-153.c: The book also lists Ficus (fig) as a sorosis; a fig is a syconus (the other option here), not a sorosis.

39-154.r: Cotton fibre → from the fruit (cotton bolls; lint and fuzz fibres); sunn, hemp and jute fibres come from stems.

39-155.r: Triticale → first man-made cereal: wheat (Triticum) × rye (Secale); self-pollinating like wheat.

39-157.r: Surfaces without soil (rock) → only lichens and mosses survive (no true roots; mosses have rhizoids); not ferns or mushrooms.

39-158.r: Eurythermal → tolerate a wide temperature range; stenothermal → narrow range; microthermal → low temperatures; hekistothermal → polar cold.

39-159.r: Desert plants have long roots (A true) because roots grow in search of water, not because hot soil boosts growth (R false); such plants: phreatophytes.

39-161.r: Phreatophytes → deep-rooted desert plants with long (20-30 ft) tap roots that reach the water table (phreatic zone).

39-162.r: Xerophytes → plants adapted to dry climate: cactus, opuntia, madar, nerium.

39-163.r: Desert plants → generally succulent (store water for dry times).

39-164.r: Epiphytes grow on other plants (e.g. trees) only for mechanical support; they take moisture and nutrients from air, rain and debris.

39-165.r: Halophytes → salt-loving plants of saline soils (mangrove swamps, marshes, seashores); hydrophytes → aquatic plants.

39-168.r: Lithophytes → plants growing in or on rocks (epipetric or epilithic plants).

39-169.r: Wrong pair: Nepenthes – hydrophyte; Nepenthes is a carnivorous tropical pitcher plant. Correct: Cuscuta–stem parasite, Chandan–root parasite, orchids–epiphyte.

39-170.r: Correct: weeping jelly from excess acid; cytokinin breaks dormancy. Wrong: sugarcane biofertilizer is Acetobacter diazotrophicus (not Rhizobium); salt-water plants are halophytes (not thallophytes).

39-171.r: Plants and animals living on land → terrestrial (habitats: forests, grasslands, deserts, mountains).

39-172.r: Producers (autotrophs) → intermediaries between biotic and abiotic components.

39-173.r: Primary productivity → rate at which green plants store solar energy as food (biomass) by photosynthesis, measured e.g. as g/m²/year.

39-174.r: Decomposition → breakdown of dead organic matter into simple inorganic substances by microbes (bacteria, fungi = decomposers).

39-175.r: Wrong pair: Herbivore – secondary consumer; herbivores eat plants. Correct: autotroph–producer, heterotroph–consumer, saprotroph–decomposer.

39-176.r: Trophic level I → green plants (autotrophs) that make food using the sun's radiant energy.

39-177.r: Primary producers in ocean food chains → cyanobacteria and diatoms; copepods are primary consumers (eat phytoplankton); foraminifera are not producers.

39-178.r: Fish survive under a frozen lake because only the top layer freezes; water below stays liquid.

39-179.r: Fish die out of water because they cannot breathe: gills absorb oxygen dissolved in water, not oxygen from air.

39-181.r: Red colour of apple → anthocyanin pigment.

39-182.r: Tomato red → lycopene (a carotenoid); apple red → anthocyanin; carrot red-orange → β-carotene.

39-185.r: Yellow colour of papaya (Carica papaya) → caricaxanthin; its papain enzyme helps digest protein.

39-186.r: New banana species Musa indandamanensis (about 11 m tall, orange pulp) → found by BSI in Little Andaman's Krishna-Nalah forest.

39-187.r: Chinese, Americans, Indians and Black Africans → one species, Homo sapiens; tigers/lions/cats etc. are different species.

39-188.r: Fungi lack chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise; now a separate kingdom (earlier counted as plants).

39-189.r: Yeast, moulds and mushrooms → fungi (no chlorophyll, no vascular bundle).

39-193.r: Gucchi (morel) → a costly fungus (family Morchellaceae) growing in some Himalayan forests; it cannot be cultivated commercially (statement 3 wrong).

39-194.r: Herpes simplex virus–human → parasitism, more exactly endoparasitism (it lives and multiplies inside human cells); the book accepts both (a) and (d).

39-195.r: Hyperparasitism → a parasite whose host is itself a parasite; common in wasps (Hymenoptera), true flies (Diptera) and beetles (Coleoptera).

39-196.r: Commensalism → one organism benefits, the other is neither harmed nor helped (+/0).

39-197.r: Fig → coevolved one-to-one mutualism with its partner fig wasp, its only pollinator.
